decisions.evidence: Risk is the initial-topology construction itself: existence, the finite-intersection basis, the empty intersection X, and the claim of containment in the norm topology. The text cites def-initial-and-final-topology for exactly those clauses and bases norm-continuity of members of X* on their boundedness; it explicitly does not claim point separation without a norming hypothesis and uses no choice.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Read all steps: the displayed finite-disk sets are weakly open and every weakly open neighborhood of x contains one (shrink each scalar disk and take the smallest radius); the seminorm p = max_j |f_j| proves continuity of addition and of joint scalar multiplication with the estimates p(av-a0v0) <= |a|p(v-v0) + |a-a0|p(v0) and the 1/(p(v0)+1) bookkeeping. The m = 0 and zero-vector cases are handled, and no choice is used.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Traced the single HB use: a norming functional on x-y gives |f(x)-f(y)| = ||x-y|| = d, and the two d/3 disks are disjoint weak neighborhoods. The zero space is vacuous, HB is declared in the statement, and cor-relative-hahn-banach-dual-norming supplies precisely the norming functional consumed.

Risk is the asserted equivalence between topological convergence and coordinate-wise eventual convergence for nets. A weak neighborhood of x is reduced to finitely many inverse disks, each contributing an eventual index, and finite directedness supplies a common upper bound; the empty intersection is handled by nonemptiness of the index preorder. No choice is used and uniqueness is deliberately not claimed without separation.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked that the displayed evaluation-disk sets form a weak-star neighborhood base, that p = max_j |h(x_j)| makes the topology a locally convex vector topology with the joint scalar continuation estimate, and that Hausdorffness follows from separation of functionals by evaluations without HB or choice.

Risk is the equivalence with finitely many evaluation conditions and the placement of the limit. The proof uses one-evaluation neighborhoods in one direction and a common upper bound for the finitely many eventual indices in the other; the asserted limit is required to lie in X* and uniqueness is derived from equality of all evaluations, not assumed.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Verified the finite-dimensional factorization: continuity at zero gives finitely many f_j and a kernel-included neighborhood, the rule l(Av) = L(v) is well-defined on the image of A, extension by zero on added standard basis vectors represents L as a finite combination of the f_j, and the reverse inclusion is immediate. Only finite basis choices occur.

Risk is the finite-dimensional factorization that represents a weak-star continuous L as an evaluation, plus uniqueness. Continuity at zero places L in the span of the finitely many defining evaluations by extending a basis of the image (choice-free, finitely many vectors); uniqueness uses HB point separation of X* on X, and the statement separates this cost from the choice-free existence.

Risks are the separation step and the closure comparison. The norm closure of a convex set is convex (approximation on both variables, endpoints included), separation of an exterior point gives a real level between Re f(x) and Re f(C), and {Re f > a} is a weak neighborhood by weak continuity of bounded functionals; the empty set is treated separately.

Risks are infinite-dimensionality for producing a nonzero common-kernel direction and reaching the sphere without leaving the ball. Given finitely many functionals, m+1 independent vectors exist by finite induction and a nontrivial dependence gives a nonzero vector killed by all of them; along that direction the norm attains 1 on a bounded segment by the intermediate value theorem. Both inclusions are proved.

Risk is applying uniform boundedness when X need not be reflexive or complete. The proof views J_X x_n as bounded maps on the Banach dual X*, obtains pointwise boundedness from convergent scalar sequences (finite head plus tail), applies the sequential uniform boundedness theorem under Countable Choice, and translates back by the HB isometry; the weak-star case applies the same theorem directly on the Banach predual with no bidual step.

Risk is an unbounded net and the extended liminf. For each dual unit-ball f, eventual scalar convergence bounds a tail infimum below by |f(x)| - eps; taking the supremum over the unit ball and using the HB norm formula gives the inequality, with the infinite case and x = 0 handled explicitly.

Risks are both directions. In finite dimension the coordinate functionals are bounded and ||v|| is dominated by the sum of coordinate moduli, so norm balls contain weak neighborhoods; in infinite dimension m+1 independent vectors give a nonzero common-kernel vector whose real multiples make every basic zero-neighborhood norm unbounded, so the bounded unit ball cannot be weakly open. Choice-free.

Risk concentrates in turning a countable local base into a countable algebraic span of X* and in the ZF Banach-space Hamel-basis theorem. Countable Choice is applied once to the finite defining lists; the finite-order factorization of each weakly continuous functional shows X* is the span of the chosen functionals; the greedy scan yields a Hamel basis, and the infinite alternative is excluded by the choice-free theorem that a Banach space has no countable Hamel basis. HB enters only in the final injectivity step.

Risk lies in the closure statements and in identifying the double annihilator with a closure. Kernels of evaluations and functionals are closed in the respective topologies in ZF, so both annihilators are closed subspaces; the weak-star double annihilator is the cited bipolar identity, while for linear M the primal identity uses HB uniform separation of a point outside the norm closure, where real-part boundedness on a real subspace forces the functional to vanish there.

Risk is the second clause: continuity of T* for the weak topologies (not merely the weak-star topologies). The first-part subbasis argument applies to the bounded map T*, whose duals are Y** and X**; the composition Phi o T* is bounded by ||Phi|| ||T||. Zero maps and zero spaces obey the same estimates.

Risks are the converse preadjoint construction and uniqueness. For fixed x, f -> (Sf)(x) is a weak-star continuous linear functional on Y*, so the HB-based duality identifies a unique Tx; linearity follows by point separation and boundedness from the dual norm supremum. The forward implication is pointwise and choice-free, as stated.

Risk is the definition by two initial topologies and the convergence equivalences. SOT is initial for T -> Tx and WOT for T -> f(Tx), which identifies WOT with the weak topology on each slice; net convergence is obtained by one coordinate test plus a common upper bound for the finitely many eventual indices. No uniformity in x is claimed and zero spaces are covered.

Risk is only the hierarchy of operator convergences. Norm convergence gives ||(T_i-T)x|| <= ||T_i-T|| ||x||, and strong convergence gives |f((T_i-T)x)| <= ||f|| ||(T_i-T)x||; the eps/(1+norm) bookkeeping covers x = 0 and f = 0, with no choice.

Risk is reaching b in ell-q without citing a duality theorem. The verification tests a bounded F on the vector with coordinates conjugate(b_k)|b_k|^{q-2} and derives sum |b_k|^q <= ||F||^q from boundedness on finite segments; b_k -> 0 for every F is exactly weak nullity, while ||e_n||_p = 1 rules out norm convergence.

Risk is only producing the detecting functional and ruling out any limit. The summation functional is bounded with norm one and equals one on every e_n, so e_n is not weakly null; coordinate evaluations kill every candidate limit, so no weak limit exists.

Risk is the duality identification over both fields. The verification derives the isometry directly for real scalars and cites the complex bilinear isometry; E_n(x) = x_n -> 0 for each fixed x in ell-1 gives weak-star nullity, and ||E_n|| = 1 is witnessed by e_n.

Risk is distinguishing the two topologies on ell-1 = (c_0)*. The coordinate units converge to zero against every vector of c_0 by definition of c_0, while the bounded summation functional has value one on every e_n, so no weak limit exists; equal topologies would have the same convergent sequences and limits.

Risks are placing 0 in the weak closure while keeping every weakly convergent sequence inside the set. Against a basic zero-neighborhood, missing the set forces sum_j |F_j(e_n)|^2 >= eps^2/n for every n, contradicting square-summability by the harmonic series; sequential weak limits have bounded norms by the uniform boundedness theorem under HB and Countable Choice, so their indices lie in a finite set, whose weak closure is itself.

Risk is representing every bounded functional on ell-2 by its coefficient sequence and controlling the shifted tails. Testing F on conjugates of e_k gives b in ell-2, whence |F(R^n x)| <= ||x|| (sum_{j>=n} |b_j|^2)^{1/2} -> 0; SOT fails at e_0, where every R^n e_0 has norm one.

Risk is only the exact value of the operator norm. Tails tend to zero for each fixed x, giving SOT convergence and ||L^n|| <= 1, while L^n e_n = e_0 witnesses ||L^n|| >= 1 for every n; the witness varies with n, which is compatible with pointwise convergence.

Risks are pointwise boundedness on a non-complete domain with unbounded norms and the incompleteness check. T_n(x) = n x_n has norm n and is eventually zero on each finitely supported x (so the sequence even converges weak-star to zero), while the truncated harmonic sequence is Cauchy in the sup norm with the non-finitely-supported harmonic sequence as its only possible limit.

Risk is the directed index construction that carries its own witnesses. The triples (U,n,x) with x in U and ||x|| >= n are directed by reverse inclusion and increasing n (using the norm-unboundedness of weak neighborhoods for a common upper bound); the net converges weakly to zero because later indices carry points inside the given neighborhood, and its norms are eventually above any bound. Including all admissible points replaces any choice function.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the definition of D(Omega) as compactly supported smooth functions, the equivalence with smooth zero extensions into Omega, the vector-space operations, the empty-domain convention, and the bilinear pairing convention. The topology is explicitly deferred to the following definitions.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the seminorms p_m, the weighted metric d, and the claim that the topology is generated by the p_m. Topology/metric agreement and completeness are deliberately deferred to the following lemma, and the empty-K and empty-interior-K cases are disposed of correctly.

Risk is that the seminorm-generated topology must coincide with the finest locally convex topology making the inclusions continuous. The definition uses all seminorms continuous on each fixed-support stage; the universal-property lemma proves that any locally convex topology with continuous inclusions is contained in this one, that the induced stage topologies are the prescribed ones, and that the construction is independent of the chosen exhaustion.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the definition as continuous complex-linear functionals on the LF test space, the bilinear pairing convention, closure under sums and scalar multiples, the empty-domain case, and the explicit deferral of the finite-order characterization and the sequential criterion to proved items.

Risks are well-definedness of the pairing and dependence only on the a.e. class. The integral is bounded by sup|phi| times the compact-support integral of |f|; linearity in both slots is pointwise, and continuity is deliberately deferred to the embedding theorem, which carries the Countable Choice cost for injectivity. The definition itself is choice-free.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the definition (u*phi)(x) = <u(y), phi(x-y)>, the safe domain {x : x - supp phi is contained in Omega} and its openness by covering the compact translated support with finitely many balls, the vanishing conventions, and the deferral of differentiability and signs to the smoothness theorem.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the rational-ball cutoff construction (finite subcover of K, product formula 1 - prod(1-b_j) equal to one on the inner balls), the exhaustion K_j, the shell cover H_j, the least-code subcover rule, and the locally finite partition whose supports are each contained in a cover member. Every selection is finite or fixed by a least code; ZF claim is honest.

Risks are the metric-topology agreement and completeness. The weighted metric is compared directly with the seminorm balls (including the tail estimate that fixes Cauchy sequences), and a d-Cauchy sequence has uniformly Cauchy zero extensions for every derivative; the limits are defined pointwise, identified as derivatives by the uniform-derivative-limit theorem, and convergence of finitely many derivatives gives p_m -> 0.

Risks are the universal property, equality of the induced stage topologies, and exhaustion-independence. The proof verifies the vector-topology axioms for the seminorm family, notes that each p_m is the restriction of the global seminorm Q_m and that Q_0 separates points, proves the map criterion by pulling back generating seminorms, and shows any other locally convex topology with continuous inclusions is contained in this one.

Risk is continuity of differentiation, smooth multiplication, translation and diffeomorphic composition on the LF space. Each is bounded on every fixed-support stage (derivatives by p_{m+|alpha|}, multiplication by the Leibniz constant, translation by an isometry, composition by the chain-rule induction); the universal property upgrades stagewise continuity to LF continuity, and the inverse operations give the isomorphism claims.

Risk is the equivalence with the quantifier order forall K exists (m_K, C_K) and the scaling step. Continuity of each restriction at zero yields one finite-order bound by taking the largest order and smallest radius of a basic neighborhood; conversely a compactwise estimate is a neighborhood condition at zero for each restriction, and the universal property upgrades it to continuity. Zero seminorms and empty stages are handled.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked that the set of admissible orders is nonempty by the compactwise finite-order characterization, that the least element exists by well-ordering of the naturals, and the definitions of global finite order, global order, and the zero-distribution conventions including the vanishing-on-D_K case.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the signed-transpose definition <d^alpha u, phi> = (-1)^{|alpha|} <u, d^alpha phi>, its continuity through the continuous test derivative, the conventions for alpha = 0 and for one coordinate derivative, and the explicit deferral of classical compatibility to the differentiation theorem.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the definition <au, phi> = <u, a phi>, its continuity and linearity via the continuous test multiplier, the algebraic identities verified on every test, and the bilinear convention with no conjugation; the absence of a product of two arbitrary distributions is stated.

Risk is the induction with signed derivatives. The first-order identity follows from the signed transpose and the ordinary product rule for tests; the identity d_i d^gamma u = d^{gamma+e_i} u uses commutativity of smooth test partials; the induction closes with Pascal's identity on multi-indices, and all sums are finite.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked continuity of delta_a through the admissible seminorm q(phi) = |phi(a)| and the derivative formula with its order-|alpha| bound on each fixed-support stage, together with the empty-domain convention for a permitted point.

Risks are glueing over an arbitrary cover without selecting labels and the finite-order estimate for the glued functional. A locally finite partition with compact supports decomposes each test finitely; independence of the containing cover member is compatibility on overlaps; the estimate sums the finitely many relevant member bounds with the Leibniz constant. Uniqueness follows from the same finite decomposition, and the empty cover is handled.

Risk is that support is defined through the largest vanishing open set and that tests agreeing near the support pair equally. Locality from the sheaf theorem makes the union of all vanishing open sets vanishing, and a test vanishing on a neighborhood of the support lies in that union; the equivalence with empty support and the compact-support terminology are stated with the relative-closedness caveat.

Risk is transferring the fixed-order estimate from a compact neighborhood to arbitrary tests. A cutoff equal to one near the support makes (1-chi)phi vanish near the support, so pairings agree; the local bound on the cutoff support plus the Leibniz expansion controls chi phi by the derivatives of phi on that compact neighborhood, and the same exponent works on every fixed-support stage.

Risks are the Taylor annihilation argument at shrinking scale and uniqueness of coefficients. A test whose jet through order m vanishes at a is cut off at scale eps and shown to pair to zero by uniform little-o bounds; the monomial tests q_alpha reproduce the jet and isolate each coefficient, and the exact-support claim uses locality.

Risk is the equivalence between boundedness and common compact support plus derivative bounds. The forward direction builds one admissible seminorm from shell suprema whose boundedness forces only finitely many shells to be occupied; the converse bounds any admissible seminorm by p_m on the common stage, and the weights are defined by suprema, so no choice is used.

Risk is that the sequence criterion is a theorem, not a definition. The forward direction uses boundedness of a convergent sequence to obtain one compact support and then the induced stage topology; the reverse direction collects the finitely many initial supports into a compact L and applies stage convergence with the continuous inclusion. Nets are correctly not covered.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the seminorm definitions for the weak and strong distribution topologies, the finiteness of p_B(u) from continuity plus absorption of a bounded set, the identification of the bounded test sets with the common-support derivative-bounded sets, the convergence descriptions, and the Hausdorff claims.

Risks are injectivity modulo a.e. equality and continuity into the strong topology. Continuity is the order-zero estimate over the common compact support of a bounded test set; injectivity convolves chi f with a normalized bump and applies the L^1 approximate identity under Countable Choice, then covers Omega by countably many rational balls. The choice cost is isolated in the cited mollifier theorem.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the implication: a singleton test set is bounded by the bounded-set characterization, so the strong seminorm evaluated at the singleton is exactly the weak pairing difference and tends to zero. The zero test, empty domain and the absence of a converse for arbitrary nets are stated.

Risks are the disjointified grid cells and the comparison of simple-function integrals with Darboux sums. Cells between the interior and the closure have the box volume, so the step functions squeeze the Lebesgue integral of g between all lower and upper Darboux sums; Riemann integrability identifies the squeeze value, and the complex case is componentwise. Countable Choice is used only through the measure interface.

Risks are the mixed-derivative identity, continuity in both distribution topologies, and classical compatibility. Mixed derivatives commute because test partials do; weak and strong continuity are identities between the associated seminorms; classical compatibility reduces to one-coordinate integration by parts on a box with Riemann-Lebesgue comparison under Countable Choice, and the multi-index case iterates.

Risks are smoothness of the parameter function, the integral clause, and the interchange. Smoothness uses uniform continuity of parameter derivatives on a compact parameter set with one common slice support; the integral clause approximates by finite grid sums that are tests, uses completeness of D_K for the limit, and identifies every derivative of the limit with the integrated derivative. All grids are specified by a least-level rule.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the safe-domain verification through the compact set H - S contained in Omega, the application of the parameter-pairing lemma to F(x,y) = phi(x-y), and the two derivative identities in which the sign of the distributional derivative and the sign of the reflected test cancel.

Risk is the Baire-category step and its exact cost. On each D_K the pointwise-bounded family is a countable union of closed sets E_j, so Baire under Dependent Choice gives one with interior; scaling at an interior point gives the uniform bound. Pointwise limits of nets drawn from the family inherit the bound; the sequence case needs no boundedness of a general net, and that limitation is stated.

Risk is that (phi/J_F) o F^{-1} is a legitimate test and that the definition is compatible with functions. The reciprocal Jacobian is smooth and positive and diffeomorphic composition is continuous on tests, so the transpose is a distribution; the change-of-variables computation (under Countable Choice for the Lebesgue interface) gives F^* u_f = u_{f o F}.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked the candidate <u tensor v, Phi> = <u, x -> <v, Phi(x,·)>>, the smoothness and compact support of the inner pairing through the parameter-pairing lemma, the values on product tests, and the explicit deferral of continuity, uniqueness and the reversed iterated order to the tensor theorem.

Risks are independence of the cutoff, continuity in the smooth-function topology, and uniqueness. Two cutoffs differ by a factor vanishing near the support; the cutoff transfer gives a finite-order bound in the q_{K,m} seminorms; tests are dense in that topology because a single cutoff on the finite union of constraints reproduces every prescribed derivative there, which yields uniqueness of the extension.

Risk is multiplying a weakly convergent sequence by a locally uniformly convergent multiplier sequence. The uniform finite-order bound under Dependent Choice controls u_j on the fixed test support, the Leibniz bound sends p_m((a_j-a)phi) to zero, and the remaining term is weak convergence tested on the fixed test a phi.

Risk is that ambient closedness is what makes the complement open and hence usable in the sheaf glue. The proof glues u on Omega with the zero distribution on the complement of F over their overlap, where u already vanishes because its support lies in F; restriction and support of the extension, and uniqueness, follow from the sheaf properties.

Risks are recovering u from L and the converse continuity. u(psi) = L(psi-check)(0) is a distribution because reflection is continuous on tests and evaluation at zero is continuous for the compact-open topology; translating gives the convolution representation and evaluation at zero gives uniqueness; conversely one compact support controls all target derivatives through the finite-order estimate.

Risk is passing from real Radon-Nikodym densities to a bounded complex density and then from bounded functions to all of L^1. Level sets {h > M + 1/k} are null by the norm bound, giving |h| <= M a.e. and |g| <= 2M; bounded complex f is handled by complex linearity, and general f by explicit truncation with dominated convergence. AC enters only through the cited real supplier.

Risks are the repeated-integration formula on a box, the Hahn-Banach extension by Zorn, and the transfer to a primitive. The kernel formula bounds p_m by the L^1 norm of T psi and gives injectivity of T; Zorn extends the real-linear functional dominated by the hemiseminorm, with the explicit one-step extension inequality; the final step integrates the density against a cube primitive and matches signs. Constants and norms are nonzero by construction.

Risk is turning the localized representation into a global identity and expanding the multiplier derivative. A cutoff equal to one near the compact support makes u = theta d^alpha u_f globally; the binomial expansion with alternating signs collapses by (1-1)-type coordinate sums to the left side, leaving finitely many continuous coefficients supported in the prescribed open neighborhood.

Risks are local finiteness of the coefficient supports and interchange of the two locally finite sums. Partition supports are enlarged with distances min(1/i, dist/2), which keeps the enlargements locally finite and compactly inside Omega; each localized distribution is compactly supported so the primitive lemma applies; on each test both sums are finite, and AC pays for the countable selection of representations.

Risks are smoothness of the convolution integral and the diagonal choice of grids. Derivative integrals arise as uniform limits of tagged sums, substitution identifies them with the convolution, and the grid level for each scale is chosen by a least-index rule; all supports stay in one compact product, so the sequence criterion for test convergence applies. Only Riemann integrals are used.

Risks are continuity of the candidate, density, support equality, and associativity. The compactwise estimate combines the two factor bounds through the parameter-pairing lemma; density of finite product sums identifies the two pairing orders and proves associativity in two stages; support equality uses local vanishing in each factor and product tests as witnesses; derivatives use the tensor derivative formula.

Read the authored text and every numbered step. Checked compactness of E_psi = (S x T) ∩ a^{-1}(supp psi) under one compact factor, the existence of the cutoff, the bilinearity conventions, and the correct deferral of cutoff independence and continuity to the following lemma.

Risks are cutoff independence, continuity on each compact, and the support inclusion. Differences of allowed cutoffs vanish on a neighborhood of the tensor support; one cutoff chosen for a target compact gives the Leibniz bound and hence continuity; the sum of supports is closed when one factor is compact, so tests supported off it have empty support intersection and pair to zero.

Risk is the interchange of integral and pairing plus uniform test convergence. The identity integral f_eps psi = u(psi_eps) uses the parameter pairing lemma on a compact neighborhood of the test support; psi_eps converges to psi in every derivative seminorm by uniform continuity and unit mass; the finite-order bound transfers the limit. No symmetry of the bump is needed.

Risks are constancy of the mollification, agreement across balls, and the nonempty-domain proviso. Vanishing first derivatives make the smooth mollification gradient-free on each ball; constants agree on overlaps by a unit-mass test; connectedness makes the locally constant value global. The empty domain is excluded because the representing constant is not unique there.

Risk is the cutoff-mollifier construction and cofinality of the exhaustion. chi_j u has compact support and extends by zero; the convolution at scale eps_j is supported in a compact subset of Omega; for a fixed test, once K_j contains its translated support the cutoff disappears and mollifier convergence gives the pairing limit. No diagonal extraction is needed.

Risks are the general two-compact-factor case and the derivative identities. The noncompact factor is split as theta q plus a remainder whose support avoids each target compact, reducing both bracketings to the all-compact case; derivative identities use the tensor derivative formula together with the vanishing of the terms that differentiate the cutoff near the tensor support; delta_0 is checked directly.

Risks are equicontinuity and the finite-net argument. Boundedness gives one compact support and derivative bounds, hence a common Lipschitz bound through the mean-value inequality; Arzela-Ascoli plus total boundedness of the closure gives finite nets for the finitely many derivative families, labelled representatives give an eps-net, and completeness of the closed set in D_K is derived from the complete metric. Countable and Dependent Choice are declared.

Risk is only the sign convention. The signed transpose gives minus the integral of phi' over [0,R] with R past the support, the FTC gives phi(0) - phi(R) = phi(0), and changing the value of H at zero does not change its a.e. class.

Risks are the locally finite break set and the sign of each jump. Only finitely many breaks meet a compact interval around the test support; integration by parts on each open piece followed by dominated convergence gives right-minus-left jumps with the correct sign, and local finiteness makes the delta sum finite on each compact, hence a distribution of finite local order.

Risks are local integrability of 1/|x|, the smooth regularization, and the ball geometry for Green's identity. Shell sums bound the singular integral; Delta N_eps = 3 eps^2 / (4 pi (|x|^2+eps^2)^{5/2}) integrates to R^3/(R^2+eps^2)^{3/2} -> 1; the eight-octant parametrization satisfies the elementary-solid clauses in every direction, and the approximate identity gives phi(0). The positive sign is checked in the final pairing.

Risks are existence of the symmetric limit and the order-one estimate. Reflection reduces the truncated integral to (phi(t)-phi(-t))/t, whose quotient extends continuously with value 2 phi'(0) and is bounded by twice the sup of |phi'|; the truncation error is O(eps), giving order at most one on each compact support. The truncated integrals are proper Riemann integrals.

Risk is the injectivity usage on the punctured domain. If delta_0 were regular, its restriction to the complement of the origin would be zero, so the density would vanish a.e. there and, the origin being null, a.e. everywhere; a test with value one at zero then contradicts the zero functional. The zero distribution is separated from the failure.

Risks are the two limits going in opposite directions. Each fixed x is eventually outside the shrinking support, so the pointwise limit is zero; the substitution t = jx - 2 turns the pairing into the integral of rho(t) phi((t+2)/j), whose deviation from phi(0) is bounded by the oscillation on a shrinking interval. The mass is one at every scale, so no pairing control follows from pointwise convergence.

Risks are nonvanishing of the derivative pairing and sharpness of the order. The monomial jet times a cutoff has alpha-derivative one at a; its rescaled copies have p_q -> 0 for q < m, so no bound of order below m can hold on a compact containing a neighborhood of a, while the order-m bound is immediate from the definition.
